items.title: Individualized Treatment Effects of Cefepime vs Piperacillin-Tazobactam in Adults Hospitalized with Acute Infection.
items.abstract: RATIONALE: Among adults hospitalized with acute infection, a recent randomized trial observed no significant average treatment effect of cefepime versus piperacillin-tazobactam on acute kidney injury or death, but fewer days-alive-and-free-of delirium and coma with cefepime. OBJECTIVES: To determine whether patients' individual characteristics modify the effect of cefepime versus piperacillin-tazobactam on outcomes. METHODS: In this secondary analysis of the Antibiotic Choice On Renal Outcomes (ACORN) trial, an effect model was derived and validated to predict the effect of cefepime versus piperacillin-tazobactam for adults hospitalized with acute infection. The primary outcome was survival without acute kidney injury; the secondary outcome was survival without delirium or coma. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: The individualized treatment effect predicted in the validation cohort significantly modified the effect of cefepime versus piperacillin-tazobactam on survival without acute kidney injury (Qini 1.68; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.25-3.18; p-value = 0.01). Among 626 patients predicted to experience ≥5% benefit from cefepime, 81.2% of patients randomized to cefepime survived without acute kidney injury, versus 74.2% randomized to piperacillin-tazobactam (difference, 7.1%; 95%CI, 0.25 to 13.9%). Among 203 patients predicted to experience ≥5% benefit from piperacillin-tazobactam, 56.6% of patients randomized to cefepime survived without acute kidney injury, versus 63.0% randomized to piperacillin-tazobactam (difference, -6.3%; 95%CI, -20.7 to 8.2%). The effect of trial group on survival without delirium or coma was not modified by individual characteristics. CONCLUSIONS: Patients' individual characteristics modified the effect of cefepime versus piperacillin-tazobactam on survival without acute kidney injury but not on survival without delirium or coma.

items.title: Pressure Points: A Scoping Review of Intracranial Pressure and Mean Arterial Pressure Measurement and Reporting Practices in Neurocritical Care.
items.abstract: Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is a cornerstone of neurocritical care, but the literature shows substantial heterogeneity in how its components-intracranial pressure (ICP) and mean arterial pressure (MAP)-are reported. We conducted a scoping review following the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR to map this variability. Structured searches in PubMed and Scopus (January 1997 to May 2026) identified 350 eligible original clinical studies. For each study, we extracted whether the ICP measurement method, ICP device, ICP zero reference, MAP measurement method, and arterial line zero reference were reported. Reporting completeness was analyzed overall and stratified by guideline era and primary diagnosis, using the χ2 tests, odds ratios with 95% CI, and the Cochran-Armitage test for trend. The ICP measurement method was reported in 84.0% of studies, and the ICP zero reference in 14.6%; the MAP method in 66.9%, and the arterial line zero reference in 28.6%. Only 6.6% of studies reported all 5 domains. After publication of the Brain Trauma Foundation fourth Edition, reporting improved across most domains-ICP method (79.0% vs. 96.1%, P<0.001) and arterial line zero reference (20.2% vs. 49.0%, P<0.001)-and the composite reporting score rose from 2.37 to 3.06 (P<0.001). ICP zero-reference reporting was similar between eras (16.5% vs. 9.8%, P=0.105) while showing a significant declining trend across the study period (Cochran-Armitage Z=-2.52, P=0.012). Traumatic brain injury and hemorrhagic conditions had the lowest ICP zero reference reporting (8.8% and 9.3%; OR=0.35 for TBI vs. non-TBI, 95% CI: 0.19-0.65). Improvements in reporting have not reached the level needed to determine whether CPP values are comparable across studies. We propose an 11-item Minimum Reporting Set for CPP-related studies.

items.title: Liberal vs. conventional pre-operative clear fluid fasting policies in children: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised and non-randomised studies.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Pre-operative clear fluid fasting in children aims to reduce the risk of pulmonary aspiration. Recent studies have shown the safety of shorter clear fluid fasting durations. However, because pulmonary aspiration is rare, it remains uncertain whether the incidence differs between the liberal (< 2 h) and conventional (≥ 2 h) clear fluid fasting policies. METHODS: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis, performing comprehensive searches across five databases. We included studies with patients aged < 18 y who underwent general anaesthesia or sedation for surgery or procedures. Primary outcome was pulmonary aspiration and secondary outcome was vomiting without pulmonary aspiration. We performed meta-analyses to estimate pooled incidences according to fasting policy (< 2 h vs. ≥ 2 h). RESULTS: We included 33 studies involving 580,197 patients. Twenty-nine studies (579,737 patients) reported pulmonary aspiration. The pooled incidence of pulmonary aspiration was 0.03% (95%CI 0.01-0.09%) with conventional fasting policies and 0.03% (95%CI 0.01-0.09%) with liberal policies. Risk ratios were available from 14 studies (475,399 patients) and showed no difference in pulmonary aspiration between policies (risk ratio 0.77, 95%CI 0.40-1.47). Seventeen studies (344,653 patients) reported vomiting; the pooled incidence was 0.99% (95%CI 0.27-3.51%) with conventional policies and 0.76% (95%CI 0.18-3.14%) with liberal policies. The certainty of evidence was very low for both outcomes. DISCUSSION: Pulmonary aspiration is rare in children, and similar incidences of aspiration and vomiting were observed under liberal and conventional clear fluid fasting policies. The results should be interpreted cautiously due to the very low certainty of evidence. items.title: Incidence and reasons for cancellation on the day of elective surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Cancellation on the day of elective surgery is a persistent challenge that compromises operating theatre efficiency, wastes resources and delays patient care. Existing evidence is difficult to interpret because definitions of cancellation vary across studies and reported reasons are classified inconsistently. We aimed to estimate the incidence of cancellation on the day of surgery and synthesise the reported reasons for cancellation. METHODS: Databases were searched for observational studies reporting elective surgery cancellations. Studies explicitly defining cancellation on the day of surgery were included in a random-effects meta-analysis of proportions. Subgroup analyses examined variation by national income level and surgical speciality, with geographical region explored in supplementary analyses. Included studies were assessed for risk of bias using Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal tools. Reported reasons were synthesised narratively across four domains: patient; medical/anaesthesia; administrative/system; and surgery/staff. RESULTS: Fifty-eight studies met the eligibility criteria, of which 37 (with a strict definition of on-the-day cancellation of surgery) were included. Pooled incidence of cancellation on the day of surgery was 14% (95%CI 13-16%), with substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 99.91%). Rates varied by national income level and surgical speciality, with higher estimates reported in low- and lower-middle-income settings and in some specialities, including ophthalmology and neurosurgery. Reasons reported most commonly included: patient declining surgery; non-fasted; unstable medical condition; changes in clinical status; improper scheduling or overbooking; instrument unavailability; and staff shortages. Sensitivity analyses supported the robustness of the findings and no clear publication bias was detected. The certainty of evidence for the pooled incidence estimate was low. DISCUSSION: Cancellation on the day of surgery remains a substantial and globally relevant peri-operative problem. Its burden and drivers are highly context-dependent and often reflect weaknesses in pre-operative preparation, organisational co-ordination and system capacity. Reducing avoidable cancellations may therefore require context-specific strategies targeting pathway reliability, timely pre-anaesthetic assessment and peri-operative resource alignment. items.title: Association of pre-operative opioid use disorder and postoperative outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Opioid use disorder may increase the risk of adverse postoperative outcomes, but the magnitude and consistency of this association remain unclear. We performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the impact of opioid use disorder on postoperative outcomes across surgical populations. METHODS: We searched electronic databases for studies comparing adults (aged ≥ 18 y) with and without opioid use disorder undergoing surgery. Primary outcomes were the incidence of any postoperative pain and composite adverse respiratory outcomes. Secondary outcomes included re-admission rates 30 and 90 days after surgery; in-hospital mortality; duration of hospital stay; and total healthcare costs. RESULTS: From the 40 included studies, three reported postoperative pain, and 19 reported respiratory outcomes. People with opioid use disorder had higher odds of postoperative pain (OR 2.87, 95%CI 1.63-5.06) and composite adverse respiratory events (OR 2.10, 95%CI 1.64-2.68), both with moderate certainty. Subgroup analyses showed increased risk of pulmonary embolism, pneumonia and other respiratory and pulmonary complications (low to moderate certainty). Low certainty evidence indicated higher 30-day and 90-day re-admission rates, prolonged duration of hospitalisation and higher total healthcare costs associated with opioid use disorder, while in-hospital mortality did not differ significantly (very low certainty). DISCUSSION: Our results suggest that opioid use disorder is associated with higher incidence of postoperative pain, increased postoperative complications and greater total healthcare costs, which supports the need for routine pre-operative screening for opioid use disorder and the application of patient-centred, multidisciplinary peri-operative care and pain management. WHAT WE DID: We looked at research studies that compared adults with and without opioid use disorder who had surgery. We combined the results from 40 studies to see whether opioid use disorder was linked to problems after surgery, including pain, breathing problems, hospital readmission and length of hospital stay. items.title: Childhood Exposure to General Anesthesia For Surgery: Identification of a Subtle Post-Operative Cognitive Phenotype.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Early-life exposure to general anesthesia has not been consistently associated with overall cognitive deficits, yet its impact on executive functions and visuo-spatial processing remains unclear. The primary objective was to assess executive function performance, according to general anesthesia exposure for surgery. The secondary objectives were to explore distinct cognitive profiles and their associated factors, as well as to examine visuo-spatial attention as a complementary domain. METHODS: In this ambidirectional cohort study, 77 children aged 9-11 years, with or without prior general anesthesia exposure for surgery, completed a cognitive battery yielding eight cognitive measures assessing inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, working memory, and visuo-spatial attention. Measures were analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model. Exploratory latent profile analysis was used to identify cognitive performance profiles. RESULTS: No significant main effect of general anesthesia exposure for surgery was observed (χ²(1) =.01, p =.92), indicating comparable overall executive function performance between exposed (mean age at exposure: 4.47 ± 3.00 years) and non-exposed. Latent profile analysis identified two executive function profiles: Efficient and Vulnerable Executive Control. General anesthesia exposure was associated with lower odds of belonging to the Efficient profile group (OR = 0.71, 95% CI [0.705, 0.710], p <.001). Regarding visuo-spatial attention, GA-exposed participants showed higher Global-Local precedence measures (estimate = 0.53, 95% CI [0.04, 1.01], p =.036). CONCLUSIONS: Early childhood exposure to general anesthesia was not associated with reduced overall executive function. However, a potential post-operative cognitive phenotype is suggested by a reduced likelihood to belong to an efficient executive control profile with greater visuo-spatial global-local precedence.

items.title: Cost-effectiveness analysis of total intravenous vs. inhalation anaesthesia among adults aged ≥ 50 y undergoing major non-cardiac surgery.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Total intravenous and inhalational anaesthesia are used widely to maintain general anaesthesia for major non-cardiac surgery, yet their comparative cost-effectiveness remains uncertain. The VITAL trial evaluated clinical outcomes, showing no difference in days alive and at home at 30 days. We conducted an economic evaluation alongside VITAL to determine whether total intravenous anaesthesia offers an economic advantage within the UK NHS. METHODS: A within-trial economic evaluation was conducted from the NHS and personal social services perspective over a 6-month time horizon. Resource use was collected from trial records and questionnaires, and health-related quality of life was measured using EuroQol five-dimension five-level instrument at baseline, discharge, 30 days and 6 months. Costs were evaluated using national sources and quality-adjusted life years were calculated using the area under the curve approach. Incremental cost-effectiveness ratios were estimated using imputed datasets, with uncertainty explored through bootstrapping and the probability of cost-effectiveness illustrated using a cost-effectiveness acceptability curve across a range of willingness-to-pay thresholds. RESULTS: A total of 2507 patients were allocated randomly: 1253 (50%) received total intravenous anaesthesia; and 1254 (50%) inhalational anaesthesia. Mean costs and quality-adjusted life years were similar across groups. Incremental cost was -£145 (95%CI -£1510-£1220) and incremental quality-adjusted life years -0.001 (95%CI -0.008-0.005). Total intravenous anaesthesia showed a 56-57% probability of cost-effectiveness at standard willingness-to-pay thresholds. Sensitivity analyses, including complete-case and societal-perspective models, yielded consistent findings of equivalence. DISCUSSION: Total intravenous and inhalational anaesthesia show comparable cost-effectiveness for adults aged ≥ 50 y undergoing major non-cardiac surgery. Given clinical equipoise and equivalent economic outcomes, anaesthetic choice should continue to be guided by patient factors, clinician expertise and organisational context. Further research may be justified given the large population undergoing major surgery. items.title: Lung Health after Preterm Birth: Knowledge Gaps and Respiratory Care Across the Lifespan.
items.abstract: Prematurity affects approximately 10% of live births worldwide and contributes to substantial short and long-term morbidity, particularly respiratory disease. Approximately 35% of infants born before 32 weeks gestation are diagnosed with bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD). Many preterm infants regardless of BPD diagnosis also develop respiratory problems in both childhood and adulthood, more recently termed as prematurity-associated lung disease (PLD). As survival of preterm infants continues to improve, the lifetime burden of PLD and related health conditions remains high. Optimizing lung growth, minimizing the impact of comorbidities, and improving quality of life are ongoing challenges. Individuals born preterm are also at higher risk for being diagnosed with early-onset chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in adulthood. Despite these public health implications, outpatient management is often variable, and PLD remains underrecognized and heterogeneous across clinical settings. In this expert consensus statement from the BPD Collaborative, we summarize key knowledge gaps and provide pragmatic recommendations to help standardize outpatient care for PLD across the lifespan. Recommendations address models of care delivery, approaches to disease monitoring and management, and the evaluation and treatment of common comorbidities. Given limited high-quality evidence in several domains, many recommendations are necessarily based on expert opinion. Our objectives are to highlight priorities for future research, promote continuity between pediatric and adult care, and support development of evidence-based strategies to reduce underdiagnosis and undertreatment and to improve long-term outcomes for individuals born preterm.

items.title: Frailty patterns in European surgical patients: The FRAGILE multicentre prospective cohort.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Frailty represents a multidimensional decline in physiological reserve that increases vulnerability to surgical stress. Its perioperative dynamics and association with outcomes across diverse surgical populations remain insufficiently characterised. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to describe the prevalence of frailty before and after surgery and to evaluate its association with postoperative complications, mortality, and hospital length of stay. METHODS: We conducted a prospective, multicentre European cohort study including adults undergoing elective or emergency surgery under general or regional anaesthesia across 64 participating centres in 10 countries. Each centre contributed data from one to three predefined recruitment days between April 2021 and December 2022. Frailty was assessed preoperatively and at 30 days using the Rockwood Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS), the FRAIL questionnaire, and the Barthel Index. The primary outcome was the association between preoperative frailty and 30-day postoperative complications (Clavien-Dindo ≥ II); secondary outcomes included 30-day mortality, postoperative cognitive impairment, and new-onset frailty. RESULTS: Among 1472 patients (mean age 60.9 years; 52.9% male), preoperative frailty prevalence was 14.6% (FRAIL), 10.4% (CFS), and 10.4% (Barthel). Within 30 days, 11.9% of nonfrail patients became frail, increasing overall frailty prevalence to 21.2%. Postoperative complications occurred in 19.2% and mortality in 1.7%. Preoperative frailty was independently associated with complications: adjusted odds ratio (OR) 2.35 [95% confidence interval (CI) 1.53 to 3.60], P < 0.001); 30-day mortality OR 10.9 (95% CI 1.28 to 93.0), P = 0.029). Frailty was also associated with postoperative cognitive impairment: OR 3.47 (95% CI 1.98 to 6.08), P < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Frailty is common among surgical patients, increases after surgery, and independently predicts postoperative complications and mortality. These findings highlight frailty as a dynamic and potentially modifiable marker of surgical vulnerability that should be routinely assessed and integrated into perioperative care. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04140370.

items.title: Postoperative delirium and 1-year functional decline, institutionalization and mortality.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Postoperative delirium is a common and serious complication in older surgical patients and has been associated with increased morbidity, healthcare costs, long-term functional decline and mortality. OBJECTIVE: To determine whether postoperative delirium is associated with functional status, quality of life, institutionalisation and mortality at 1 year after surgery in a large multicentre surgical cohort. DESIGN: Prospective multicentre observational study. SETTING: Forty-three hospitals in Spain. Surgical patients were recruited in November 2023 and assessed for delirium 48 h after surgery, with follow-up at 1 year. PATIENTS, OTHER PARTICIPANTS: A total of 2442 adult surgical patients undergoing elective or urgent procedures requiring hospital admission. Postoperative delirium was assessed using the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM), CAM for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) or the telephone-administered 4AT according to clinical setting. INTERVENTIONS: None. MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Functional status and quality of life at 1 year assessed using the 12-item World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule (WHODAS 2.0). Secondary outcomes included institutionalisation and mortality. RESULTS: After excluding 81 deaths and 462 nonresponders, the 1-year telephone follow-up was completed for 1899 patients. Postoperative delirium within the first 48 h was independently associated with a 4.6-point higher WHODAS score at 1 year: adjusted mean difference = 4.60 [95% confidence interval (CI), 1.57 to 7.64, P = 0.003]. Delirium was also associated with increased institutionalisation and higher mortality: odds ratio (OR) 2.5 (95% CI, 1.07 to 5.84, P = 0.03), and (16.7 vs. 3.1%; P < 0.001), including 30-day, 60-day, and 365-day mortality (all P < 0.001), respectively. CONCLUSIONS: Postoperative delirium is independently associated with long-term functional decline, loss of independence, institutionalisation and increased 1-year mortality. These findings highlight delirium as a key perioperative complication and support prevention strategies and structured long-term follow-up after surgery. TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier: NC-T06127901).

items.title: Persistent Genito-pelvic Pain 2 Months after Vaginal Birth: A Nationwide Population-based Analysis from the 2021 French National Perinatal Survey.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Persistent pain can significantly affect maternal health outcomes. However, there is a lack of representative data after vaginal birth. This study used population-based data to estimate the prevalence and risk factors of persistent genito-pelvic pain 2 months after vaginal birth. METHODS: Data from the 2021 National Perinatal Survey, a French nationwide, cross-sectional, population-based survey, were analyzed. The study population included women who delivered vaginally. The main outcome was persistent genito-pelvic pain at 2 months postpartum after vaginal birth. Prevalence with 95% CIs was estimated overall and by degree of perineal tear. Risk factors were identified on univariable and multivariable logistic regression. All analyses were weighted to account for 2-month attrition. RESULTS: Among 5,802 vaginal births, the prevalence of persistent genito-pelvic pain at 2 months postpartum was 12.8% (95% CI, 11.8 to 13.8%), ranging from 5.9% (4.3 to 7.9%) for women with no tear to 38.9% (27.1 to 52.2%) for those with obstetric anal sphincter injury. On multivariable analyses, persistent pain was significantly associated with all degrees of perineal tear versus no tear (first/second-degree tears: adjusted odds ratio, 2.08 [95% CI, 1.51 to 2.87]; episiotomy: 3.37 [2.27 to 4.99] and obstetric anal sphincter injury 5.92 [3.03 to 11.55]). Other risk factors included being born in Africa (1.51 [1.06 to 2.16]), primiparity (1.50 [1.20 to 1.87]), poor maternal psychological status during pregnancy (2.05 [1.48 to 2.83]), and operative birth (1.43 [1.14 to 1.79]). Negative childbirth experience (2.03 [1.50 to 2.77]) and dissatisfaction with pain management during the maternity stay (somewhat satisfied: 1.59 [1.28 to 1.98]; and little/not at all satisfied: 3.11 [2.27 to 4.26]) were also associated with persistent pain. CONCLUSIONS: At 2 months postpartum, persistent genito-pelvic pain affected one in eight women after vaginal birth and increased with perineal injury severity. Further studies are warranted to explore the potential preventive effects of limiting perineal tears and instrumental births on persistent pain, optimizing maternal satisfaction with postpartum pain management, and improving childbirth experience.

items.title: Impact of clinical frailty on mortality after elective surgery in patients aged ≥ 90 years admitted to critical care: a binational intensive care registry analysis.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Increasing numbers of patients aged ≥ 90 years require elective surgery. Frailty is increasingly recognised as a key determinant of peri-operative risk, but high-quality evidence to understand the impact on outcomes in this age group is limited. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society Adult Patient Database. Patients aged ≥ 90 years admitted to ICU following elective surgery were included, encompassing planned and unplanned ICU admissions. Frailty was assessed at ICU admission using the Clinical Frailty Scale and patients categorised as non-frail or frail. Propensity score matching was performed to balance age; sex; acute illness severity; and comorbidities. Primary outcome was 1-year all-cause mortality. Secondary outcomes included ICU mortality; in-hospital mortality; return to pre-admission residence; and ICU and duration of hospital stay. RESULTS: The matched cohort comprised 5398 patients (2699 without frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale 1-4) and 2699 living with frailty (Clinical Frailty Scale 5-8)), with good post-matching covariate balance. Mortality in ICU was low and not significantly different between patients who were frail and non-frail. Frailty was independently associated with higher in-hospital mortality (matched hazard ratio (HR) 1.66, 95%CI 1.22-2.27, p = 0.001) and higher 1-year mortality (matched HR 1.66, 95%CI 1.47-1.87, p < 0.001). Patients without frailty had higher odds of returning to their pre-admission residence at hospital discharge than patients living with frailty (matched OR 1.45, 95%CI 1.29-1.62, p < 0.001). Patients who were frail experienced longer hospital stays and higher rates of postoperative complications, including delirium and acute renal failure. DISCUSSION: Among patients aged ≥ 90 years undergoing elective surgery with postoperative intensive care admission, frailty is strongly associated with prolonged recovery and worse short and long-term outcomes. Incorporation of frailty assessment into peri-operative pathways may improve risk stratification, shared decision-making and personalised care for patients aged ≥ 90 years. items.title: Intra-operative hypotension threshold models and subdistribution hazard of postoperative pneumonia in patients having non-cardiac surgery.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Intra-operative hypotension is common during general anaesthesia, but its association with postoperative pneumonia remains uncertain, partly because hypotension has been defined using different thresholds. We evaluated whether absolute thresholds or relative reductions from baseline mean arterial pressure were associated more strongly with postoperative pneumonia after non-cardiac surgery. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective multicentre cohort study of 151,036 adults undergoing non-cardiac surgery under general anaesthesia at three Chinese hospitals. Intra-operative hypotension was assessed using 12 metrics across nine thresholds, including absolute mean arterial pressure thresholds of < 50 mmHg to < 70 mmHg and relative reductions of 20-50% from baseline. The primary outcome was postoperative pneumonia within 30 days. RESULTS: Of 151,036 patients, postoperative pneumonia occurred in 3486 (2.3%). Relative reductions in mean arterial pressure were more consistently associated with postoperative pneumonia than absolute thresholds. At a 20% reduction from baseline, the number of intra-operative hypotension episodes was associated with postoperative pneumonia (subdistribution hazard ratio (sHR) 1.079, 95%CI 1.050-1.109, p < 0.001), as was the presence of intra-operative hypotension (sHR 1.108, 95%CI 1.068-1.149, p < 0.001). Absolute thresholds were not consistently associated with postoperative pneumonia after adjustment. Duration-related metrics were generally less consistent than depth- or recurrence-related metrics. Dose-response analyses showed that risk increased rapidly at low exposure levels and then plateaued across relative thresholds of 20-40%. DISCUSSION: Intra-operative hypotension was associated with postoperative pneumonia when defined as a relative reduction from baseline mean arterial pressure, whereas conventional absolute thresholds were less informative. These findings suggest that maintaining intra-operative blood pressure close to baseline may be more relevant to pulmonary risk than relying on fixed absolute thresholds alone. items.title: The Association Between Early Arterial Oxygen Tension and in-Hospital Mortality in Patients With Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage Admitted to ICUs in Australia and New Zealand: A Retrospective Multicenter Cohort Study.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Variable systemic oxygenation may affect mortality in critically ill patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH). METHODS: In this multicenter retrospective cohort study, data were extracted from the Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society Adult Patient Database. Adult patients with aSAH admitted to an intensive care unit (ICU) between January 2018 and June 2024 were included. The arterial oxygen tension during the initial 24 hours in ICU (D1 PaO 2 ), which yielded the highest Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation III-J oxygenation subscore, was the primary exposure variable. The primary outcome was in-hospital mortality. A multivariable mixed-effects logistic regression model was constructed to determine the adjusted probability of in-hospital mortality based on D1 PaO 2 . RESULTS: A total of 6446 patients were included. The median D1 PaO 2 was 92 mm Hg (IQR: 74 to 138), in-hospital mortality was 20.0% (n=1291), and 12-month mortality was 25.6% (n=1647). A U-shaped multivariable relationship was observed between D1 PaO 2 and in-hospital mortality, with 79 mm Hg being associated with a nadir of 16.2%. This varied according to age (65 y and over: 69 mm Hg; below 65 y: 83 mm Hg), admission type (medical: 77 mm Hg; surgical: 89 mm Hg), intubation status (not intubated: 90 mm Hg; intubated: 143 mm Hg), and Glasgow Coma Score (GCS) (GCS 15: 75 mm Hg; GCS 13 to 14: 65 mm Hg; GCS 7 to 12: 96 mm Hg; GCS 3 to 6: 131 mm Hg). CONCLUSIONS: In critically ill patients with aSAH, a U-shaped relationship was noted between D1 PaO 2 and in-hospital mortality. This varied according to patient demographics and illness severity.

items.title: Hyperlactatemia and Elective Tumor Craniotomy: Prospective Observational Study of Prevalence, Risk Factors, and Association With Short-Term Outcomes.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Hyperlactatemia is common during brain tumor craniotomy, although the pathophysiology and association to outcome are unclear. We prospectively investigated prevalence and risk factors for perioperative hyperlactatemia (S-lactate ≥2.2 mM) as well as its association with short-term outcomes in patients undergoing elective brain tumor craniotomy. METHODS: In 450 patients, arterial lactate was measured hourly from the first surgical incision until 6 hours postoperatively. The primary outcome was a change in the level of neurological disability, measured by the modified Rankin Scale preoperatively and at 30 days after surgery. Secondary outcomes were length of hospital stay, new neurological deficits at discharge, days alive and out of hospital at 30 days, and 30-day mortality. Hyperlactatemia was analyzed both as a dichotomous (≥1 measurement of S-lactate ≥2.2 mM) and as a continuous variable (lactate load). We used both a multivariable regression and a backward stepwise regression analysis to identify risk factors for hyperlactatemia and factors associated with postoperative outcomes. RESULTS: Hyperlactatemia was seen in 66% of the study participants. No association was found between hyperlactatemia and modified Rankin Scale change from baseline to 30 days or any other clinical outcome. Independent factors associated with hyperlactatemia were mean perioperative glucose (0.14; 95% CI: 0.09-0.18; P <0.001), preoperative glucocorticoid dose (0.09; 95% CI: 0.06-0.12, P <0.001), malignant CNS-derived tumor type (0.25; 95% CI: 0.08-0.42; P =0.004), and inverse noradrenaline dose (-0.02; 95% CI: -0.04 to -0.006, P =0.006). CONCLUSIONS: We did not find an association between perioperative hyperlactatemia and short-term outcomes in patients undergoing brain tumor craniotomy. Preoperative glucocorticoids, perioperative glucose, malignant CNS tumor, and noradrenaline dose were independently associated with hyperlactatemia.

items.title: Incidence, Predictors, and Outcomes of Early Postoperative Dysnatremia After Pediatric Neurosurgery: A Prospective Observational Study.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Sodium abnormalities are frequent in the neuro intensive care unit (ICU) settings. Dysnatremia can also manifest in the perioperative period in neurosurgical patients and can lead to adverse consequences. The burden of dysnatremia following elective pediatric neurosurgery is unclear. Hence, we aimed to assess the incidence, risk factors, and outcomes of dysnatremia in children undergoing elective neurosurgeries. METHODS: This was a single-center, prospective observational study in consecutive elective pediatric neurosurgical patients aged < 18 years. Perioperative data were collected for the first 3 postoperative days and included age, gender, weight, American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status classification, location of surgical pathology, preoperative sodium, intraoperative blood loss and transfusion, intraoperative fluid balance, balanced salt solution use, perioperative vomiting, steroid use, seizures, Glasgow coma scale score, duration of ICU and hospital stay, and in-hospital mortality. Hyponatremia was defined as serum sodium < 135 mEq/L, hypernatremia as serum sodium > 145 mEq/L, and dysnatremia as the presence of either hyponatremia or hypernatremia. RESULTS: Six hundred sixty-eight children who underwent neurosurgery had perioperative sodium values assessed during the 22-month study period. The incidence of postoperative dysnatremia was 18.6% (124/668). In multivariate regression analysis, sellar/suprasellar region pathologies, preoperative dysnatremia, and higher blood loss were predictors of postoperative dysnatremia. Children with postoperative dysnatremia had a higher occurrence of seizures, neurological deterioration, and death, and longer ICU and hospital stays. CONCLUSIONS: About one-in-five children undergoing neurosurgery develop postoperative dysnatremia, and it is predicted by preoperative dysnatremia, sellar/suprasellar pathology, and higher blood loss. Dysnatremia is associated with poor clinical outcomes. STUDY REGISTRATION: Clinical Trials Registry-India: CTRI/2022/01/039795.

items.title: Global Neurointensive Care: A Field Yet to Be Born.
items.abstract: Neurological conditions represent the leading cause of disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) and the second leading cause of death globally, with more than 11 million deaths annually, 87% of which occur in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). While global neurosurgery has emerged as a recognized field with dedicated frameworks for advocacy and action, the critical care continuum of neurological disease has been persistently overlooked. Global neurointensive care (GNIC) does not yet exist as a formally defined discipline, yet its need is urgent and measurable: ICU bed density in LMICs ranges from 0.1 to 2.5 per 100,000 inhabitants compared with 5 to 30 per 100,000 in high-income countries (HICs); a cross-sectional survey of 408 providers from 42 LMICs found that only 36.8% had access to a dedicated neurointensive care unit; and traumatic brain injury (TBI) mortality at 6 months exceeds 37% in Latin American LMICs. This viewpoint defines GNIC, characterizes the epidemiological and structural dimensions of the unmet need with granular supporting evidence, reviews existing initiatives and their limitations, and proposes a 6-domain strategic agenda for its development. GNIC must be established as a field parallel and complementary to global neurosurgery, ensuring the critical care continuum of neurological disease is not abandoned in the global effort towards universal health coverage.

items.title: Infiltration between the popliteal artery and the capsule of the knee (IPACK) vs. selective tibial nerve block for analgesia after total knee arthroplasty: a triple-blinded randomised controlled trial.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Infiltration between the popliteal artery and the capsule of the knee (IPACK) and the selective tibial nerve block provide analgesia for the posterior aspect of the knee after total knee arthroplasty. This randomised controlled triple-blinded trial tested the hypothesis that IPACK provides superior analgesia to selective tibial nerve block after total knee arthroplasty. METHODS: Patients having total knee arthroplasty under spinal anaesthesia with a femoral triangle block were allocated randomly to receive either IPACK with 19 ml ropivacaine 0.2% or a selective tibial nerve block with 5 ml ropivacaine 0.75%. The postoperative analgesic strategy included paracetamol; ibuprofen; and intravenous morphine patient-controlled analgesia. Primary outcome was cumulative intravenous morphine consumption on postoperative day 1. Secondary analgesic outcomes included pain scores at rest and during movement measured on postoperative days 1, 2 and 3. Functional outcomes were quadriceps strength; walking distance; and range of motion. RESULTS: In total, data from 90 patients were analysed (45 allocated to each group). Cumulative intravenous morphine consumption on postoperative day 1 was similar between the patients allocated to the IPACK and selective tibial nerve block groups (mean (SD) 6 (7) mg vs. 5 (6) mg, respectively; p = 0.36). Four patients (9%) who received selective tibial nerve block had motor block of the common peroneal nerve. No other differences were seen between groups in secondary outcomes. DISCUSSION: The IPACK and selective tibial nerve block provide similar analgesia after total knee arthroplasty under spinal anaesthesia with a femoral triangle block. items.title: Infiltration between the popliteal artery and the capsule of the knee (IPACK) vs. selective tibial nerve block for analgesia after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a randomised controlled trial.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Infiltration between the popliteal artery and the capsule of the knee (IPACK) and the selective tibial nerve block both provide analgesia for the posterior aspect of the knee after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. This randomised controlled triple-blinded trial tested the hypothesis that IPACK provides superior analgesia to a selective tibial nerve block after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction. METHODS: Eighty patients having anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction under general anaesthesia with a femoral triangle block were allocated randomly to receive either IPACK with 20 ml ropivacaine 0.2% or a selective tibial nerve block with 5 ml ropivacaine 0.75%. Postoperative analgesia included paracetamol, ibuprofen and intravenous morphine patient-controlled analgesia. Primary outcome was cumulative postoperative intravenous morphine consumption at 24 h. Secondary pain-related outcomes included pain scores at rest and on movement at 2 h, 24 h and 48 h. Early functional outcomes evaluated were range of motion; quadriceps strength; and walking distance measured at 24 h and 48 h. Late functional outcomes included concentric quadriceps strength and single-hop test, measured at 4 months and 8 months. RESULTS: Median (IQR [range]) cumulative intravenous morphine consumption at 24 h postoperatively was similar between IPACK (12 (6-20 [0-54]) mg) and selective tibial nerve block (16 (10-30 [0-66]) mg, p = 0.073). No significant differences between groups were seen in the secondary pain or functional outcomes. No complications were reported. DISCUSSION: The IPACK and selective tibial nerve block provide comparable postoperative analgesia after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction under general anaesthesia with a femoral triangle block, with similar impact on functional outcomes. WHAT WE DID: We studied 80 patients having surgery to repair a torn knee ligament, called the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL). All patients had a general anaesthetic and another nerve block. They were then randomly given either an IPACK block or a tibial nerve block to help control pain at the back of the knee. We compared their pain, how much morphine they needed and how well they could move and use their leg. WHY WE DID IT: Pain at the back of the knee can be a problem after ACL surgery. An IPACK block and a tibial nerve block can both help with this pain. We wanted to find out whether the IPACK block gave better pain relief than the tibial nerve block.

items.title: Cranial Electrotherapy Stimulation for Fibromyalgia in Veterans: A Randomized Sham-Controlled Feasibility Study of Resting-State Functional Connectivity Magnetic Resonance Imaging to Evaluate Pain and Treatment Response.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain disorder frequently co-occurring with depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and insomnia, particularly in veterans, and safer nonpharmacological therapies are needed. Cranial electrotherapy stimulation, also referred to as cranial electrotherapy stimulation (CES), may help with anxiety and sleep, but its effect on pain is unclear. This feasibility study evaluated magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to identify neural correlates of pain and treatment response for CES effects on fibromyalgia pain in veterans. METHODS: In a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial at a single US government hospital, veterans aged 20 to 60 with fibromyalgia were assigned to active or sham in-home CES, stratified by sex. Participants self-administered CES for 60 minutes daily over 12 weeks. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was acquired at baseline, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks with clinical outcomes, including the Defense and Veterans Pain Rating Scale (DVPRS), National Institutes of Health (NIH) Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) measures, and tests of physical function. RESULTS: Forty-eight participants were randomized (25 active, 23 sham) and 47 were analyzed. Both groups showed significant improvements in DVPRS pain (-1.88 ± 2.2) and pain interference with sleep (-2.25 ± 2.8), mood (-1.88 ± 2.6), activity (-1.83 ± 2.4) and stress (-1.77 ± 3.0) at 12 weeks versus baseline (P < .01), with significant between-group differences only in sleep (P = .04). Neuroimaging revealed significant increases in connectivity between the cerebellar 7b seed and the left occipital fusiform gyrus (0.079 ± 0.1) left lingual gyrus (0.063 ± 0.08), and right lingual gyrus (0.058 ± 0.08) for the CES group and decreases in the sham group (-0.088 ± 0.1; -0.121 ± 0.08; and -0.135 ± 0.1), respectively. No adverse events occurred. CONCLUSIONS: Both groups improved similarly in pain and function, though new analgesic usage was more prevalent in the sham group. Neuroimaging revealed differential changes in cerebellar-sensory-visual networks and baseline patterns distinguishing responders from nonresponders, supporting feasibility and design of larger, adequately powered CES trials in fibromyalgia.

items.title: Comparison of Paravertebral Block and Serratus Posterior Superior Intercostal Plane Block for Postoperative Analgesia After Video-Assisted Thoracoscopic Surgery: A Prospective, Randomized Controlled Trial.
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare the analgesic efficacy of serratus posterior superior intercostal plane block (SPSIPB) versus thoracic paravertebral block (TPVB) in patients undergoing video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS), with a focus on postoperative opioid consumption and pain scores. DESIGN: A prospective, randomized, controlled, single-center clinical trial. SETTING: A tertiary university hospital. PARTICIPANTS: Sixty adult patients aged 18 to 80 years scheduled for elective VATS. Participants were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to receive either SPSIPB (n = 30) or TPVB (n = 30). Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups. INTERVENTIONS: Prior to induction of general anesthesia, patients received either ultrasound-guided SPSIPB or TPVB using 30 mL of 0.25% bupivacaine. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: The primary outcome was cumulative 24-hour postoperative opioid consumption, expressed as oral morphine equivalents. Secondary outcomes included numeric rating scale (NRS, 0-10) for pain scores and the incidence of opioid-related adverse effects at 1, 3, 6, 12, and 24 hours after surgery. Twenty-four-hour opioid use was not significantly different between SPSIPB and TPVB (66.8 ± 29.4 mg v 77.2 ± 40.0 mg; mean difference -10.4 mg; 95% CI, -36.1 to 15.3; p = 0.439). No significant differences were seen in pain scores or opioid-related side effects at any assessed time point (p > 0.05). CONCLUSIONS: SPSIPB and TPVB were associated with similar postoperative opioid consumption, pain scores, and the incidence of adverse effects following VATS. Given its potentially simpler application, SPSIPB may serve as an effective alternative regional analgesic technique in thoracic surgery.

items.title: Sex, Racial, and Ethnic Reporting in Regional Anesthesia Trials for Joint Arthroplasty: A Systematic Review of Published Versus ClinicalTrials.gov Data.
items.abstract: Regional anesthesia provides significant perioperative benefits, including improved pain control and reduced opioid consumption. Clinical trial evidence underpins anesthetic practice, yet inadequate demographic representation and reporting may limit the ability to likely evaluate findings and perpetuate inequities. This systematic review assessed the reporting of race, ethnicity, and sex in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of regional anesthesia for total joint arthroplasty (TJA). The Aggregate Analysis of Clinical Trials (AACT) database was searched for US-based interventional RCTs of regional anesthesia for TJA published from 2015 to 2025. Trials were required to be registered and published in English. Exclusion criteria included conference abstracts, duplicate publications, and non-peer-reviewed reports. Data on trial characteristics, sample size, interventions, and participant demographics were compared from published articles and ClinicalTrials.gov. The primary outcome was reporting of participant sex, race, and ethnicity in publications and registry entries. Secondary outcomes included demographic distributions across racial and ethnic groups and associations between reporting and study characteristics (funding source, year of publication, center type, US region, sample size) using Fisher's exact test. Twenty-nine RCTs were included in the final analysis, representing 2914 participants. Of 29 journal articles, 28 studies (96.6%) reported sex, 14 (48.3%) reported race, and five (17.2%) reported ethnicity in the published journal articles. Among studies reporting race, 1068 (78.5%) participants identified as White, 253 (18.6%) as Black, 30 (2.2%) as other, 6 (0.4%) as Asian or Pacific Islander, and one (0.07%) as Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander. Conversely, the data from ClinicalTrials.gov reveals that of the same 29 studies, 22 (75.9%) reported sex, 12 (41.4%) reported race, and seven (24.1%) reported ethnicity. Trial characteristics did not show statistically significant associations when comparing studies that did versus did not report race, ethnicity, or sex. In this review of demographic reporting of US-based regional anesthesia RCTs for TJA, sex was consistently reported, whereas race and ethnicity were infrequently captured. The lack of difference in reporting practices across various trial characteristics points toward a broader issue within the field of regional anesthesia for TJA. items.title: Pain management after total shoulder arthroplasty: a systematic review and procedure-specific postoperative pain management (PROSPECT) recommendations.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Total shoulder arthroplasty is associated with moderate-to-severe postoperative pain. The aim of this systematic review was to assess the available literature and provide PROSPECT (PROcedure SPECific Postoperative Pain ManagemenT) recommendations for optimal pain management after total shoulder arthroplasty. METHODS: A systematic review utilising PROSPECT methodology was performed. Randomised controlled trials and systematic reviews published in the English language that assessed postoperative pain using analgesic, anaesthetic and surgical interventions were identified from databases. RESULTS: Of the 1809 articles identified, 30 randomised controlled trials and seven systematic reviews/meta-analyses met our inclusion criteria. Interventions that improved postoperative pain relief included: paracetamol and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; dexamethasone; interscalene brachial plexus block and, as an alternative, local infiltration analgesia. Conflicting evidence was found for continuous interscalene brachial plexus block (catheter) or liposomal bupivacaine for interscalene block or local infiltration analgesia. No evidence was found for a specific surgical technique. DISCUSSION: In the absence of contraindication, the analgesic regimen should include: paracetamol; a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug administered peri-operatively and continued postoperatively; intravenous dexamethasone (8-10 mg); and postoperative opioids for rescue analgesia. As a regional technique, an interscalene brachial plexus block with a single-bolus injection of long-acting local anaesthetic (bupivacaine or ropivacaine), but not liposomal bupivacaine, should be provided. In case of contraindications or absence of expertise, local infiltration analgesia is a reasonable alternative. Further studies are required to investigate the analgesic benefit of a continuous infusion for the interscalene brachial plexus block. We reviewed 30 randomised trials and seven reviews of previous studies to find out which treatments gave patients the best pain relief. We wanted to find the best ways to control this pain and provide clear advice for doctors and other healthcare staff. items.title: The analgesic efficacy of opioids in different application modalities for the treatment of breakthrough cancer pain-a systematic review with network meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Breakthrough cancer pain episodes often require oral immediate release opioids or parenteral opioid treatment. Different formulations and application modalities have been approved for this condition. This study aimed to identify the most effective of the available substances and applications to treat breakthrough cancer pain. We conducted a comprehensive systematic review with network meta-analysis. The database search included MEDLINE, CENTRAL, Embase, and Web of Science. Eligible were randomized controlled trials comparing opioids and application modalities for the treatment of breakthrough cancer pain episodes. Primary end points were the pain intensity difference (PID) at 15 and 30 minutes. Secondary end points were side effects and adverse events, as well as dichotomous outcomes of treatment success. Frequentist network meta-analysis was conducted using the package netmeta in R. From 5133 records initially identified by the literature review, 23 studies were eligible for quantitative analysis. Compared with placebo, the most effective interventions at 15 minutes (PID) were intravenous or subcutaneous applications of morphine, and intranasal fentanyl or sublingual fentanyl tablets. After 30 minutes (PID), the most effective interventions were still subcutaneous and intravenous morphine, but also sublingual fentanyl tablets. Intranasal fentanyl spray was equally effective as buccal and other transmucosal applications by 30 minutes. The quality of evidence on the topic is poor as most studies are phase III trials for drug approval. The risk of publication bias is therefore high. Sublingual fentanyl tablets were as effective as intravenous or subcutaneous morphine and are a practical modality for self-administration.

items.title: Canadian evidence-based guidelines on spinal procedures for chronic pain.
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Interventional procedures are commonly used to diagnose and treat chronic pain of spinal origin but guidance on: their indications; frequency; technical conduct; requirements for image guidance; outcome measurement; and management of complications is lacking. These guidelines were developed by a Canadian group of clinicians, researchers, patient partners and representatives from provincial healthcare regulatory and funding bodies. METHODS: Reviews of published literature were undertaken for commonly performed spinal procedures for pain, and the evidence was synthesised qualitatively. Evidence-based recommendations for each procedure were graded on a scale from A (strongest level) to D (not recommended), or as insufficient (I), using US Preventive Services Task Force criteria with the level of certainty rated as high, medium or low. All consensus recommendations required at least 75% agreement among the guideline panel. Good clinical practice statements were also developed. RESULTS: We provide 15 key recommendations. The guidelines provide clinical practice recommendations and good clinical practice statements for procedures targeting chronic pain originating from the cervical, lumbar spine and sacroiliac joints. Clinical indications, evidence for efficacy and suggested frequency for repeated procedures have also been proposed. DISCUSSION: These guidelines provide evidence-based recommendations and good clinical practice statements for performing diagnostic and therapeutic spinal interventions for chronic pain. WHAT WE DID: A group of doctors, researchers, patients and healthcare organisations from Canada looked at research about procedures used to diagnose and treat long‐lasting pain coming from the spine. They reviewed the evidence and worked together to agree on recommendations for how these procedures should be carried out safely and effectively. WHY WE DID IT: Many different procedures can be used to help people with long‐lasting back or neck pain, but there was not enough clear guidance about when they should be used, how often they should be repeated and how they should be performed. We wanted to create clear advice based on the best available research. items.title: Brain gray matter changes across chronic pain trajectories: MRI evidence from 35,000 individuals.
items.abstract: Chronic pain affects brain gray matter structure, but the magnitude, pattern, and reversibility of brain changes upon pain recovery remain unclear because of inconsistent findings from small-scale studies. We analyzed data from 35,052 UK Biobank participants who completed chronic pain assessments at 2 time points, approximately 9 years apart, evaluating pain lasting 3 months or more, across 8 body sites. Brain magnetic resonance imaging data were available from the second time point. Participants were grouped into 4 categories: Pain-free controls, New chronic pain, Persistent chronic pain, and Resolved chronic pain. We examined relationships between these categories and 313 brain-wide measures across cortical surface area, cortical thickness, and subcortical volume. New chronic pain was associated with surface area reductions in sensorimotor, temporo-parietal, and medial and lateral prefrontal cortices. Persistent chronic pain showed larger and more widespread area reductions and mixed changes in cortical thickness and subcortical volumes, including cerebellar atrophy and hypertrophy in the thalamus and basal ganglia. Resolved pain demonstrated reversibility of most brain changes, except sustained surface area reductions in the primary somatosensory cortex. No areas showed effects consistent with a predisposition to pain. Brain structural changes in chronic pain reflect adaptive neuroplasticity rather than irreversible damage or preexisting vulnerability. Most changes appear reversible with pain resolution, underscoring the importance of effective pain treatment to alleviate symptoms and support recovery of brain structure and function.

items.title: Intrathecal Hydromorphone Dosing for Adolescent Spinal Fusion: A Prospective Dose-Escalation Study.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intrathecal opioids are widely used for postoperative analgesia in pediatric spine surgery, but optimal dosing remains undefined. We evaluated the relationship between intrathecal hydromorphone (ITH) dose, analgesia, and adverse effects in adolescents undergoing posterior spinal fusion (PSF). METHODS: In this single-center, prospective, blinded dose-escalation study using a biased-coin up-down sequential allocation design, patients aged 10-17 years undergoing PSF received ITH starting at 3.5 mcg kg-1, with dose adjustments based on analgesic response (range 2.0 to 7 mcg kg-1 with a maximum of 400 mcg). The primary outcome was maximum postoperative pain within 18 h. Secondary outcomes included pain burden (area under the curve), 24-h systemic opioid consumption (oral morphine equivalents [OME], excluding ITH), adverse effects, supplemental diazepam use, and rescue opioid use. Associations between dose and outcomes were assessed using Spearman correlation and logistic regression. RESULTS: Twenty-seven patients completed the study. The median ITH dose received was 5.5 mcg kg-1 (IQR, 3.5-7.0), with a median absolute dose of 370 mcg (IQR, 180-400). No significant association was observed between ITH dose and maximum pain (r = 0.16, p = 0.41), pain burden (r = 0.32, p = 0.10), or 24-h OME (r = 0.13, p = 0.52). ITH dose was not significantly associated with the time to rescue opioid (HR = 1.24; 95% CI 0.68-2.25; p = 0.485) or diazepam (HR = 1.10; 95% CI 0.72-1.71; p = 0.655). Adverse respiratory events occurred at doses > 5 mcg kg-1 without improved analgesia. CONCLUSIONS: Increasing ITH dose was not associated with improved analgesia or change in supplemental opioid or diazepam use. Doses > 5 mcg kg-1 were associated with adverse respiratory effects. These findings support conservative dosing strategies and underscore the need to define the minimum effective dose in pediatric populations.

items.title: Contemporary Survey of the Impact of Perioperative Catastrophes on Anesthesiologists.
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Perioperative catastrophes are sentinel events in anesthesiology with well-described emotional and professional consequences. A landmark national survey published in 2012 demonstrated substantial and prolonged distress among anesthesiologists after such events. Since 2012, anesthesiology practice has evolved within a healthcare environment characterized by persistent workforce strain, heightened attention to clinician well-being, and expansion of peer support programs. A contemporary reassessment is warranted. METHODS: A voluntary, anonymous electronic survey was distributed in 2025 to U.S.-based members of the American Society of Anesthesiologists (Schaumburg, Illinois) who had opted to receive research surveys. The 44-item instrument was adapted from the 2012 questionnaire to preserve longitudinal comparability while incorporating contemporary support modalities. Domains included experience with perioperative catastrophes, characteristics of a memorable event, emotional and physical sequelae, impact on clinical performance, recovery trajectories, and perceptions of institutional support. Descriptive analyses were performed. RESULTS: Of 1,725 respondents included in analysis (response rate, 7.1%), 94.2% reported involvement in at least one perioperative catastrophe during their careers. After a memorable event, 72.5% reported physical symptoms, and 91.6% reported psychosocial symptoms. Most respondents perceived impairment in ability to provide anesthesia care in the first 4 h (69.0%) and 24 h (61.5%) after the event. Nearly one fifth (19.7%) reported never fully recovering emotionally, closely mirroring rates reported in 2012. Although informal peer support was common, formal debriefing and institutionally supported time off were infrequently provided. Nearly one quarter of respondents reported considering leaving anesthesiology as a result of a perioperative catastrophe. CONCLUSION: Perioperative catastrophes remain a common experience in anesthesiology and continue to carry substantial and enduring consequences. Despite increased cultural awareness, there remains a gap between recognition of their impact and clinicians' reported recovery experiences. Routine integration of peer support, nonpunitive debriefing, and flexible duty relief may represent critical opportunities to improve clinician well-being, patient safety, and workforce sustainability.

items.title: Centrally mediated pain features predict persistent pain in early inflammatory arthritis: a 2-year prospective study.
items.abstract: Patients with inflammatory arthritis (IA) often report pain not necessarily coupled to active inflammation. We previously demonstrated that a significant subset of patients with newly diagnosed IA report features of centrally mediated pain. In this prospective study following the same IA cohort, we tracked the relative contributions of inflammatory/noninflammatory mechanisms to pain over 2 years. We used patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), clinical data (including ultrasound), and standardised quantitative sensory testing. Mixed-effects regression models examined longitudinal associations. We recruited 66 patients. At 6, 12, and 24 months, 62%, 57%, and 49% of individuals, respectively, reported persistent pain (numerical rating scale ≥3). Using factor-derived composite scores, baseline and longitudinal inflammation was not associated with subsequent pain ( b -0.05, P = 0.87), whereas higher centrally mediated pain markers predicted less pain reduction ( b 1.41, 95%, P < 0.001). Baseline PROMs of centrally mediated pain (fibromyalgia severity average marginal effect [AME]: 0.94, P < 0.001, painDETECT AME: 1.03, P < 0.001) and mental health (eg, Generalised Anxiety Disorder-7 AME: 1.08, P < 0.001) were the strongest predictors of persistent pain. Baseline trapezius pressure pain threshold (PPT) and conditioned pain modulation (CPM) pain detection threshold (PDT) effect showed modest association (trapezius PPT AME: -0.51, P = 0.054, CPM PDT effect AME: -0.49, P = 0.051) whereas temporal summation of pain (AME: 0.09, P = 0.756) and CPM pain tolerance threshold effect (AME: -0.01, P = 0.964) did not. In our cohort, persistent pain was associated with higher baseline and longitudinal scores for centrally mediated pain according to PROMs rather than inflammation according to joint ultrasound. In IA, early identification and treatment of features of centrally mediated pain may improve pain-related outcomes.

items.title: Verbally induced placebo effects on heat pain tolerance in preschool-aged children.
items.abstract: Unlike in adults and older children, placebo hypoalgesia has not been experimentally studied in preschool-aged children. Because of their cognitive developmental stage and sensitivity to adult-provided cues, this age group may be particularly susceptible to pain modulation through verbal suggestions. Similar to a typical clinical context, we examined verbally induced placebo effects in 117 children aged 3 to 6 years using a developmentally adapted heat pain tolerance task. A placebo condition ("magical" analgesic cream) was compared with either a control cream or a natural history condition. Behavioral (heat pain tolerance [HPTol]) and self-reported pain outcomes were assessed. Child and parental characteristics were evaluated as potential predictors of the placebo effect. Significant placebo effects on HPTol were observed compared with both control conditions, with larger effects in the placebo vs control cream comparison. No placebo effect was found for self-reported pain. Analyses of potential predictors indicated stronger placebo effects in younger children, in those with higher inhibitory control, and in children of mothers with greater optimism. No other child or parental characteristic significantly predicted the placebo effect. This is the first report that verbal suggestions can elicit robust behavioral placebo effects on HPTol in preschool-aged children, suggesting that expectation-based interventions may be harnessed even at this early developmental stage. The larger placebo effect observed when compared with a control cream than with a natural history condition suggests that treatment contrasts may modulate placebo responding in young children. The dissociation between behavioral and self-reported measures highlights the need for multimethod pain assessment in early childhood.

items.title: One in seven has severe pain: a point-prevalence study of hospitalised patients across Africa.
items.abstract: Acute pain in hospitalised patients is common, yet African data are scarce. We conducted a prospective point-prevalence study of hospitalised adult patients across Africa to determine acute pain prevalence and severity and investigate associations of pain with critical illness and 7-day mortality. On a single day, investigators assessed patients' worst pain in the preceding 24 hours using a 0 to 10 visual-numerical scale and recorded vital signs. Critical illness was defined as ≥1 vital sign out of range, in line with an international consensus definition. In-hospital mortality was assessed at day 7. Data are presented as median [interquartile range], n (%), and odds ratios with 95% confidence intervals. Between September and December 2023, 19,438 patients from 180 hospitals in 22 African nations were included (age 40 [29; 59] years; 10,874 [56%] female). Pain prevalence [95% CI] was 67.9% [67.9-68.5], with 2795 (14.4%) patients reporting severe pain (≥7/10). Pain was more common among patients admitted for emergency or trauma care and in surgical and high-care wards. Pain severity did not differ meaningfully between sexes. There was no evidence of an association between pain severity and critical illness; however, increasing pain severity was associated with a higher likelihood of 7-day mortality. These findings are comparable to data from high-income countries despite substantial differences in healthcare resources, suggesting that acute pain remains a persistent and underaddressed problem globally. This study provides the first large-scale evidence of acute pain burden in African hospitals and lays a foundation for future research aimed at comprehensively characterising in-hospital pain.

items.title: Antepartum obstructive sleep apnea screening and its association with postpartum respiratory depression: a retrospective cohort study (2020-2025).
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Obstructive sleep apnea is not routinely screened for in the peripartum population, and its association with postpartum respiratory depression remains unclear. We evaluated positive antepartum obstructive sleep apnea screening and its association with postpartum respiratory outcomes. METHODS: We conducted a single-center retrospective cohort study of parturients undergoing routine antepartum obstructive sleep apnea STOP screening (loud snoring, daytime tiredness, observed apnea, high blood pressure) from July 2020 to June 2025. Delivery encounters with at least one STOP response were included. Positive STOP screening was defined as ≥2 criteria. Postpartum respiratory outcomes included bradypnea, oxygen desaturation, and naloxone administration. Associations of positive STOP screening, individual STOP components, and self-reported obstructive sleep apnea with postpartum respiratory outcomes were evaluated using logistic regression. RESULTS: Among 19,250 delivery encounters, 608 (3.2%) screened positive and 182 (1.0%) reported obstructive sleep apnea. Bradypnea occurred in 2.8% (532/19,237) and oxygen desaturation in 2.4% (356/14,723). Positive STOP screening was associated with desaturation (adjusted OR 1.86, 95% CI 1.21-2.88; P = 0.005), but not bradypnea. Preeclampsia or a hypertensive diagnosis was associated with bradypnea (OR 1.64, 95% CI 1.14-2.35) and desaturation (OR 2.88, 95% CI 2.06-4.03). Self-reported obstructive sleep apnea was associated with bradypnea (OR 2.01, 95% CI 1.06-3.84) and desaturation (OR 2.72, 95% CI 1.46-5.08). Snoring, tiredness, and observed apnea were associated with desaturation but not bradypnea. CONCLUSION: Positive antepartum STOP screening was associated with postpartum desaturation but not bradypnea. Preeclampsia or a hypertensive diagnosis may be an important screening question for postpartum respiratory depression.

items.title: The association between pain intensity during epidural labour analgesia and intrapartum hyperthermia: a multicentre prospective observational study
